title: Motion principles for a small system
excerpt: Use two durations and one ease to show that something changed. A button, a card, and a page with three different personalities will feel like three products.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky. The steady verticals fit a piece about motion that stays on one system.
caption: Two durations are enough to show a change. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How much motion does a small product system need?
faqs.answer: Two durations and one ease. Use the short one for hovers, toggles, and other changes under the pointer, and the longer one for panels and dialogs. Ease-out, without bounce, is enough. A third duration should be a named exception on the same card, or it should not exist.

faqs.question: Which CSS properties should animation use?
faqs.answer: Transform and opacity. They show a change without pushing the rest of the page around. Animating height, top, or margin causes layout shift. Google's Core Web Vitals guidance treats a cumulative layout shift under 0.1 as a good experience, and layout animation works against that.

faqs.question: What happens when someone prefers reduced motion?
faqs.answer: Drop the travel and keep the state change. A panel still opens, a dialog still appears, and focus still moves. Build that behavior from the same tokens as the full motion, and test with the operating system setting turned on. Deleting motion for everyone is a different design from honoring the request.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
Motion design principles for a small system fit on a card: two durations and one ease. Use motion to show that something changed. Do not give every component its own personality. A button that bounces, a card that springs, and a page that fades on a different curve will feel like three products, and they will be harder to settle when someone asks for less motion.

Write the two durations down. Use them. When a moment needs something else, resist, or change the card on purpose and revisit every existing move.

## Two durations and one ease

Pick a short duration for changes that are already under the pointer or the keyboard. A hover, a toggle, a menu item, a color change on a button. Something around 150 milliseconds is enough to see that the control responded, and short enough that it does not hold up the next click. Pick a longer duration for things that enter or leave the screen: a panel, a dialog, a disclosure that opens. Something around 250 milliseconds lets the eye catch the arrival without turning it into a scene.

These are craft numbers, not a law of physics. The point is that there are two, and that the team can remember them. A third duration for "special" moments will become a fourth by the next release. If a large route change truly needs more time, it still uses the same ease, and you add it to the card as a named exception. Unnamed exceptions are how a system dissolves.

One ease, used everywhere. A simple ease-out is enough: the movement starts a little quicker and settles. It matches the feeling of something arriving and then staying still. Ease-in, which starts slow and ends fast, feels like the object is being yanked away. A spring with bounce draws attention to the curve instead of the change. You can like bounce and still refuse it. Personality in the easing function is personality you will have to maintain on every component, including the ones that should feel quiet.

Put the values in one place in the code. A token for the short duration, a token for the long one, a token for the ease. Components use the tokens. A transition written as a raw number on a single card will drift the next time someone copies a snippet from a different file.

## Motion means something changed

The legitimate uses are small. A panel arrived. A selection moved. A toast confirmed that the save happened. A disclosure opened and the content is this content. The motion agrees with a change that also exists in the markup: a region is present, a button is pressed, a message is in the log.

If you remove the motion and the change is still obvious, the motion was doing its job. If you remove the motion and the change disappears, the motion was hiding a missing state. Fix the state. A new item in a list needs a place in the list, and maybe a short highlight. It does not need to fly in from the corner to be believed.

Do not animate to express the brand. The brand can be felt in the accent, the type, and the pace of the copy. A custom bounce on every button is a tax on use. People who live in a tool click hundreds of times a day. Multiply your favorite curve by a hundred and watch how quickly it becomes noise.

Entrance animations on a marketing page are the same rule, applied once. The headline can arrive, briefly, with the long duration. It should be present in the HTML even before it moves, and it should not block the words. A hero that withholds the sentence until a timeline finishes is a slower page and a worse one. The change you are showing is "the page is here," which the page can show by being here.

Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) include cumulative layout shift, and a good experience keeps that score under 0.1. Motion that changes layout, top, height, or margin, pushes content around and creates shift. Animate transform and opacity. They do not reflow the page. A panel can fade and move a few pixels into place without shoving the paragraph below it. If the panel takes up space, reserve the space first, then reveal. The layout stays still. The change is still visible.

## One personality, which is almost none

Components share the card. Buttons, menus, dialogs, and the mobile navigation all use the short or the long duration, and the same ease. A dialog does not get a special overshoot because it is important. Importance is the copy and the focus, which moves into the dialog and stays there until it closes.

Lists do not stagger their children by default. A stagger looks organized in a prototype and slow on a page with twenty items. If you stagger, cap it, and only on a first view a person asked for. A filter that restaggers the list every time they change a checkbox is the system showing off.

Page transitions, if you use them, are one idea. A short fade, or a shared element that actually helps the eye, such as a title that persists. A different transition per route is a personality per page. It will not survive contact with a CMS, a loading state, and a developer who has an afternoon. Prefer no route transition over a brittle one. The content arriving, fast, is the effect you wanted.

Icons that spin to mean "loading" can spin. That is a change of state, and it should stop when the state ends. An icon that bounces forever to draw the eye to a feature is an advertisement inside the product. Put the feature in the empty state sentence instead.

## Reduced motion is the same system, stopped

Some people ask their operating system for less motion. The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes WCAG as the shared standard for making web content more usable, including for people who need calmer interfaces. Honor `prefers-reduced-motion`. The two durations become no travel. Opacity can still change, briefly, or the state can swap instantly. The information stays.

Build the reduced version with the full one, not after launch. A token or a helper that returns "do not travel" is the whole implementation, if every component already uses the tokens. A page full of hand-written transitions will miss the setting in the one component somebody copied from a demo.

Autoplaying loops stop. Carousels do not advance on their own. Video waits for a choice. Parallax does not run. These are not edge cases on a marketing site that wanted to feel alive. They are the site, for the person who asked.

Test by turning the setting on and using the product. Open a menu, a dialog, and a disclosure. Nothing should cross the screen. Then turn the setting off and confirm the two durations are still there. Deleting all motion to satisfy the setting, and shipping that to everyone, means you skipped the design. Some people did not ask for less. They still deserve a clear, short confirmation that something changed.

## What you write on the card

The card is small.

- Short duration, for state under the pointer or keyboard.
- Long duration, for a panel, dialog, or disclosure.
- One ease, ease-out, with no bounce.
- Properties: transform and opacity only.
- Reduced motion: no travel, state still changes.
- Motion explains a change that exists without it.

Pin the card in the repo and in the design file. In Figma, the durations are a note on the component, not a different spring on every frame. In code, they are the tokens. A prototype that uses a custom spring "just for the review" will be copied into production if you do not forbid it. Forbid it by having nowhere to put a third value except as a change to the card.

Review new work against the card in the same pull request as the feature. A delightful transition that does not name its duration is a defect. It will be the one that runs long, shifts layout, or ignores the reduced-motion setting.

## A pass before you add any more motion

Use the product with motion on, then with the system preference set to reduce.

- You can point at which duration each move uses.
- Nothing bounces.
- Nothing animates height or top.
- A dialog is reachable and understandable with motion reduced.
- Loading motion stops when loading stops.
- The homepage sentence is readable if you never wait for the animation.

If a move fails, take it back to the card or delete it. A small system with two durations will feel more considered than a large one with a mood for every component. Considered is the personality you can actually keep.

The way those decisions live in the stylesheet is the next practical question. [What Tailwind is doing on a Hanabi site](/blog/what-tailwind-is-doing-on-a-hanabi-site) explains how spacing and type stay in the code as a small set of repeated choices. Motion tokens belong in that same small set, or they will be reinvented in arbitrary values.

If you want those durations chosen and applied with the rest of the interface, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring a screen that moves too much. The useful outcome is usually a shorter list.
